Leo did not want to spend his summer vacation pulling weeds. His mother had signed him up to volunteer at the community garden on Maple Street, and he was not happy about it. "All of my friends are swimming at the neighborhood pool," he grumbled as they walked down the sunny block together.

At the garden, an elderly woman named Mrs. Alvarez waved them over. She wore a wide straw hat, and there was dirt on both of her knees. "You must be Leo," she said with a friendly smile. "I have been waiting all week for a strong helper, and this little plot belongs to you now."

Leo stared at a small square of dry, lumpy soil that did not look like much at all. Mrs. Alvarez handed him a packet of tomato seeds and a tiny shovel. She demonstrated how to dig shallow holes, drop in the seeds, and pat the dirt down gently with his palm. "Water them every single morning," she instructed. "Plants are patient, but they are never forgetful."

For two long weeks, absolutely nothing happened. Leo watered the bare soil each day and felt ridiculous. Then one morning, he noticed tiny green sprouts poking up through the dirt. He knelt down carefully and counted twelve of them! He raced across the garden to tell Mrs. Alvarez, and she laughed and clapped her hands.

By the middle of July, the tomato plants were taller than his waist. However, one morning Leo discovered that something had chewed the leaves and nibbled two green tomatoes. He also noticed small paw prints in the mud. "Rabbits," Mrs. Alvarez said, shaking her head. Leo felt his face get hot, because all of his hard work seemed ruined.

That afternoon, Leo did not hurry home early. Instead, he located some old wire and wooden stakes behind the tool shed. He spent three hours constructing a low fence around his plot. His fingers got scratched, but he refused to stop until every gap was closed.

The fence worked perfectly. In August, Leo picked his first ripe tomato, which was warm from the sun and bright red. He carried a heavy basket to Mrs. Alvarez and offered her the biggest one.

"Next summer," Leo announced, "may I grow peppers too?"
stem: Which sentence best states a theme of the story?
choices: It is better to spend the summer with friends at the pool.
Wild animals should never be allowed near a garden.
Patience and hard work can turn something small into something rewarding.
Older people always know more than young people.
explanation: Leo waits two weeks for sprouts, fixes the rabbit problem by building a fence, and is finally rewarded with ripe tomatoes. The story shows that patience and hard work pay off.

Long ago in ancient Greece, a young woman named Arachne lived in a small village near the sea. Her family was poor, but Arachne had a special talent. She could weave cloth more beautifully than anyone in the land. Her pictures in thread showed rivers that seemed to ripple and birds that looked ready to fly away.

People came from faraway towns just to watch her work. "Surely the goddess Athena taught you this skill," they often said. Athena was the goddess of wisdom and weaving. The people of the village believed every great weaver owed her thanks.

Arachne would toss her head proudly. "Nobody taught me anything," she boasted. "My skill belongs to me alone. In fact, I am a better weaver than Athena herself. If she disagrees, let her come and try to beat me."

High on Mount Olympus, Athena heard these arrogant words. She dressed herself as a bent old woman and walked into the village. She gently warned Arachne, "Be careful, child. Ask the goddess to forgive you before it is too late." Arachne only laughed at the stranger and said her challenge again.

Suddenly the old woman vanished, and Athena stood there, tall and shining. The people dropped to their knees, but Arachne did not say she was sorry. Instead, she set up her loom, and the contest began.

Athena wove a grand scene of the gods sitting on their thrones. Arachne wove a picture that made fun of the gods and showed their mistakes. Her threads were so fine and her colors so bright that even Athena could not find a single flaw. Still, the goddess was furious that a human would mock the gods so boldly.

Athena touched Arachne lightly on the forehead. At once, Arachne began to shrink. Her arms and legs grew thin, and soon she had eight of them. Her body became small and round. Arachne had been changed into the very first spider.

"You love to weave," Athena said, "so you and your children will weave forever." From that day on, Arachne spun thin, silky webs in the corners of houses and between the branches of trees.

The people of ancient Greece told this story to remind others that talent is a gift. Even the most skillful person should stay humble.
stem: What lesson does this myth teach?
choices: People should practice every day to improve a skill.
Even very talented people should stay humble.
Spiders are helpful animals that should be protected.
explanation: The last paragraph says the story reminds people that talent is a gift and that even the most skillful person should stay humble.

In the spring of 1848, eleven-year-old Hannah Brooks left her home in Missouri. Her family had sold their farm, packed everything into a covered wagon, and joined a wagon train heading west on the Oregon Trail. Her father dreamed of rich farmland in Oregon, more than two thousand miles away.

The journey was harder than Hannah had imagined. Each day, the wagons rolled slowly across the endless prairie. Hannah walked beside the wagon for hours because the oxen were already pulling a heavy load. At night, she gathered dried buffalo chips for the cooking fire, since there were almost no trees to burn.

After six weeks, the wagon train reached a wide, muddy river. The water was brown and fast after the spring rains. The wagon master studied the river for a long time. "We cannot wait for the water to go down," he announced. "Snow will close the mountain passes if we arrive too late."

Hannah's little brother, Thomas, grabbed her hand. He was only six, and his lip was trembling. "What if the wagon tips over?" he whispered. Hannah was frightened too, and her stomach felt tight. However, she did not want Thomas to see her fear.

"Papa has crossed rivers before," she told him calmly. "We will hold on tight and sing our counting song. By the time we reach one hundred, we will be on the other side."

The men raised the wagon boxes onto blocks of wood so the water would not soak their supplies. Then Papa cracked the whip, and the oxen stepped into the cold current. The wagon rocked and creaked. Water splashed over the sides, and a sack of flour floated away. Hannah held Thomas tightly and kept counting out loud, even when her voice shook.

At last, the oxen climbed onto the far bank. The family was soaked, and they had lost some flour, but everyone was safe. Mama hugged both children and looked at Hannah with surprise. "You were so brave," she said softly.

That night, Hannah wrote in her small journal by the light of the campfire. "Today I learned that being brave does not mean you are not scared," she wrote. "It means you keep going anyway."
stem: Why does the wagon master decide NOT to wait for the river to go down?
choices: The oxen are too tired to keep walking.
Snow could close the mountain passes if they arrive too late.
The families have run out of flour.
Another wagon train is waiting behind them.
explanation: The wagon master says, "Snow will close the mountain passes if we arrive too late." That is the cause of his decision.

The journey was harder than Hannah had imagined. Each day, the wagons rolled slowly across the endless prairie. Hannah walked beside the wagon for hours because the oxen were already pulling a heavy load. At night, she gathered dried buffalo chips for the cooking fire, since there were almost no trees to burn.

Hannah's little brother, Thomas, grabbed her hand. He was only six, and his lip was trembling. "What if the wagon tips over?" he whispered. Hannah was frightened too, and her stomach felt tight. However, she did not want Thomas to see her fear.

When you flip a light switch, the room fills with light right away. It may seem like magic, but it is really science. The light turns on because electricity is moving along a path called a circuit.

Electricity is a form of energy. It is made of tiny bits called electrons that move from place to place. But electrons cannot move just anywhere. They need a complete path that forms a loop. That loop is a circuit.

A simple circuit has three main parts. First, it needs a source of energy, such as a battery. Second, it needs wires to carry the current. Third, it needs something that uses the energy, like a light bulb or a small motor. All of these parts must be joined in an unbroken loop. Then electrons can flow from the battery, through the wire and the bulb, and back to the battery again.

There are two kinds of circuits you should know about. In a closed circuit, the path is complete. The current can flow, so the bulb glows. In an open circuit, there is a gap somewhere in the path. Because the loop is broken, the electrons stop moving and the bulb goes dark. A switch is just a tool that opens and closes a circuit. When you turn a switch off, you make a gap on purpose.

Not every material lets current pass through it easily. Materials that let it flow are called conductors. Most metals, such as copper and steel, are good conductors. That is why the wires inside your walls are usually made of copper. Materials that block the flow are called insulators. Rubber, plastic, glass, and wood are common insulators. Power cords are covered with plastic or rubber. This coat keeps the current inside the wire, so it does not shock the person who is holding the cord.

Knowing about circuits helps people stay safe. Water from a river or a sink can carry current, so you should never touch a switch or plug with wet hands. You should also never poke anything into an outlet. Electricity is useful, but it can be dangerous when it goes where it should not go.

The next time you turn on a lamp, think about the hidden loop that makes it work.

Two hundred years ago, moving goods across New York State was slow and costly. Farmers in the West grew plenty of wheat and corn, but getting their crops to cities on the East Coast was a big problem. Roads were rough and muddy. Wagons pulled by horses could carry only small loads, and a trip could take weeks.

DeWitt Clinton, who later became governor of New York, had a bold idea. He wanted to dig a canal, or a man-made river, across the state. It would connect the Hudson River near Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Boats could then travel all the way from the Great Lakes to New York City by water.

Many people laughed at the plan. The canal would need to stretch about 363 miles through forests, swamps, and hills. Some people called it "Clinton's Ditch" and said it would never work. Still, Clinton did not give up, and digging began on July 4, 1817.

Building the canal was very hard work. Thousands of workers used shovels, picks, and horses to dig the long ditch. Many of the workers were new arrivals from Ireland. They cleared trees, pulled out stumps, and moved tons of dirt and rock. In some places, the land rose or fell too steeply for boats. To solve this problem, workers built locks. A lock is like a water elevator that raises or lowers a boat from one level to the next.

In 1825, after eight years of work, the Erie Canal was finally finished. Boats were pulled along the water by mules that walked on a path beside the canal. The trip that once took weeks by wagon now took about ten days. The cost of shipping goods dropped to about one tenth of what it had been.

The canal changed the country in many ways. Towns such as Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo grew quickly along its banks. New York City became the busiest port in the United States. Settlers also used the canal to travel west, which helped new states grow.

Today, trains and trucks carry most goods. However, people still ride boats on parts of the Erie Canal for fun and remember the "ditch" that changed America.

Garrett Morgan was born in 1877 in Paris, Kentucky. His parents had once been enslaved, and his family worked hard to make a living. Garrett went to school only until about the sixth grade. But he never stopped learning. He loved to find out how machines worked. He would take them apart and put them back together.

As a teenager, Garrett moved north to Ohio to look for work. He settled in the city of Cleveland and got a job fixing sewing machines. He became so skilled that he soon opened his own repair shop. Later, he started other businesses as well, such as a shop that made clothing.

Garrett was always looking for ways to solve problems. He noticed that firefighters often got sick from breathing thick smoke. So he designed a safety hood that covered a person's head. A long tube hung down near the floor, where the air was cleaner. With this hood, a person could breathe more safely in a room full of smoke. Garrett got a patent for his invention in 1914.

Two years later, his hood was put to a real test. In 1916, a blast trapped workers in a tunnel under Lake Erie. The tunnel filled with deadly gas, and rescuers could not get inside. Garrett and his brother rushed to the scene with his safety hoods. They went down into the tunnel. They helped carry several men out to safety. Because of their bravery, more fire departments became interested in his hood.

Garrett also cared about safety on the roads. In the early 1900s, cars, horses, bikes, and people all shared busy streets. Many early traffic signals had only two signs, "Stop" and "Go." They switched with no warning, so crashes were common. One day Garrett saw a bad crash. He decided to make a better signal. His design added a third position that stopped traffic in all directions for a moment. This gave drivers time to slow down before the signal changed. He got a patent for it in 1923. Later, he sold the rights to a large company.

Garrett Morgan died in 1963. Today, his ideas live on in the masks that protect rescue workers. They also live on in the traffic lights that warn drivers before they must stop at a busy corner.

Garrett Morgan was born in 1877 in Paris, Kentucky. His parents had once been enslaved, and his family worked hard to make a living. Garrett went to school only until about the sixth grade. But he never stopped learning. He loved to find out how machines worked. He would take them apart and put them back together.

As a teenager, Garrett moved north to Ohio to look for work. He settled in the city of Cleveland and got a job fixing sewing machines. He became so skilled that he soon opened his own repair shop. Later, he started other businesses as well, such as a shop that made clothing.

Garrett was always looking for ways to solve problems. He noticed that firefighters often got sick from breathing thick smoke. So he designed a safety hood that covered a person's head. A long tube hung down near the floor, where the air was cleaner. With this hood, a person could breathe more safely in a room full of smoke. Garrett got a patent for his invention in 1914.

Two years later, his hood was put to a real test. In 1916, a blast trapped workers in a tunnel under Lake Erie. The tunnel filled with deadly gas, and rescuers could not get inside. Garrett and his brother rushed to the scene with his safety hoods. They went down into the tunnel. They helped carry several men out to safety. Because of their bravery, more fire departments became interested in his hood.

Garrett also cared about safety on the roads. In the early 1900s, cars, horses, bikes, and people all shared busy streets. Many early traffic signals had only two signs, "Stop" and "Go." They switched with no warning, so crashes were common. One day Garrett saw a bad crash. He decided to make a better signal. His design added a third position that stopped traffic in all directions for a moment. This gave drivers time to slow down before the signal changed. He got a patent for it in 1923. Later, he sold the rights to a large company.

Garrett Morgan died in 1963. Today, his ideas live on in the masks that protect rescue workers. They also live on in the traffic lights that warn drivers before they must stop at a busy corner.
